title: Intersection with an ideal generated by an H1-regular sequence modulo an ideal
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative ring, let $I\subseteq A$ be an ideal, and let $g_1,\ldots,g_r\in A$, with $r\geq0$. Assume their images in $A/I$ are an $H_1$-regular sequence [def-weil-pbc-koszul-regular-sequence], that is, the first homology of their Koszul complex over $A/I$ vanishes. Set $G=(g_1,\ldots,g_r)\subseteq A$. Then $I\cap G=IG$. No Noetherian, local, proper-ideal, or nonzero-ring hypothesis is imposed; the empty sequence is allowed.

proof.text: Put $\overline A=A/I$ and write a bar for reduction. Use [lem-weil-pbc-exterior-power-free-basis] for $A^r$ and $\overline A^r$, and [def-weil-pbc-koszul-complex] for the differentials: in degrees $0,1,2$ the Koszul terms are respectively the ring, the free module on $e_i$, and the free module on $e_i\wedge e_j$ ($i<j$), with $d_1(e_i)=g_i$ and $d_2(e_i\wedge e_j)=g_i e_j-g_j e_i$. The same formulas hold with bars over $\overline A$. Define $q_n$ in these degrees by reducing each coefficient. Since reduction preserves sums and products, these formulas give $q_0d_1=\overline d_1q_1$ and $q_1d_2=\overline d_2q_2$. Each $q_n$ is surjective by lifting its finitely many coefficients, and $\ker q_1$ consists exactly of the vectors with coefficients in $I$.

source.place: Tag 0665, lemma-H1-regular-in-quotient, proof; its low-degree element chase written explicitly using Tag 0622 (definition-koszul).

proof.text: Let $x\in I\cap G$. By the definition of the ideal generated by $g_1,\ldots,g_r$, choose $a_i\in A$ with $x=\sum_i a_i g_i$. In $K_1(A,g)$ set $a=\sum_i a_i e_i$, so $d_1(a)=x$ by [def-weil-pbc-koszul-complex]. Since $x\in I$, the degree-one reduction satisfies $\overline d_1(q_1(a))=q_0(x)=0$: it is a cycle.

source.place: Tag 0665, lemma-H1-regular-in-quotient, proof; its low-degree element chase written explicitly using Tag 0622 (definition-koszul).

proof.text: By [def-weil-pbc-koszul-regular-sequence], the hypothesis is $H_1(K_\bullet(\overline A,\overline g))=0$, where homology is $\ker\overline d_1/\operatorname{im}\overline d_2$. Therefore the cycle $q_1(a)$ has zero class and belongs to $\operatorname{im}\overline d_2$: choose $\beta$ in degree two with $\overline d_2(\beta)=q_1(a)$. In the degree-two basis of step 1 write $\beta=\sum_{i<j}\overline b_{ij}(e_i\wedge e_j)$, lift each $\overline b_{ij}$ to $b_{ij}\in A$, and set $b=\sum_{i<j}b_{ij}(e_i\wedge e_j)$. Then $q_2(b)=\beta$.

source.place: Tag 0665, lemma-H1-regular-in-quotient, proof; its low-degree element chase written explicitly using Tag 0622 (definition-koszul).

proof.text: Set $c=a-d_2(b)$. The coefficient calculation from step 1 gives $q_1(c)=q_1(a)-\overline d_2(q_2(b))=0$, hence $c=\sum_i c_i e_i$ with every $c_i\in I$. By [lem-weil-pbc-koszul-differential-square-zero], $d_1d_2=0$, so $d_1(c)=d_1(a)=x$. The degree-one formula in [def-weil-pbc-koszul-complex] yields $x=\sum_i c_i g_i\in IG$. Thus $I\cap G\subseteq IG$.

source.place: Tag 0665, lemma-H1-regular-in-quotient, proof; its low-degree element chase written explicitly using Tag 0622 (definition-koszul).

proof.text: For $u\in I$ and $v\in G$, the product $uv$ belongs to both $I$ and $G$. Finite sums of such products therefore belong to $I\cap G$, proving $IG\subseteq I\cap G$ by the definition of ideal product. Combine the inclusions. If $r=0$, then $G=0$ and both sides are zero; all displayed sums and degree-two lifts are empty. For $r=1$ the degree-two term is zero, so step 3 gives $q_1(a)=0$ directly. The calculations also hold for $I=A$ and for the zero ring.
